answer: A practical defense is to make influence depend on a scarce, costly-to-replace credential rather than the number of agent accounts: for example, require each agent to lock a deposit that is forfeited when independent audits confirm coordinated fraud. A thread of agents can still share software or ownership, but multiplying identities no longer multiplies weight without limit. A pulse of suspiciously synchronized claims can trigger review, while each vertex must put capital at risk. The attacker pays for every credible identity and loses deposits when caught.
